label: Circles and Spheres
notes: Spanning printed pages 77 through 95, this chapter trades straight-line habits for the language of circles, spheres, and one point at infinity. We compute inversions, predict when lines become circles, recognize coaxal pencils, and end at stereographic projection and the elliptic plane.

label: Power of a Point
notes: The power of a point measures how far that point sits from a circle, signed by whether it lies outside or inside. Every secant or tangent drawn through the point yields the same product, which makes power a coordinate-free invariant we reuse throughout the chapter.

label: Radical Axis and Center
notes: Setting the powers with respect to two circles equal carves out the radical axis, a straight line perpendicular to the line joining their centers. Three circles taken pairwise give three radical axes that concur in a single radical center, a fact that anchors many constructions.

label: Coaxal Systems
notes: A coaxal system is a one-parameter pencil of circles sharing a common radical axis. The intersecting type passes through two fixed points, while the non-intersecting type has two limiting point-circles. Each pencil is the orthogonal family of the other, forming a curved coordinate grid.

label: Inversion in a Circle
notes: Inversion fixes a center and radius, then maps each point along its ray so the product of the two distances equals the radius squared. Points near the center fly outward, distant points move inward, the circle stays fixed pointwise, and applying the map twice restores the original.

label: Circles to Circles
notes: Treating a line as a circle through infinity, inversion sends generalized circles to generalized circles. Lines through the center stay lines, other lines become circles through the center, circles through the center straighten into lines, and all remaining circles map to circles.

label: Conformality
notes: Inversion is conformal: it preserves the magnitude of angles between curves while reversing their sense. The proof tracks tangent directions through the radial map. This angle-preserving property is exactly why orthogonal circle pencils stay orthogonal after inversion, keeping the coaxal grid intact.

label: Orthogonal Circles
notes: Two circles meet orthogonally when their tangents, equivalently their radii, are perpendicular at each intersection. Algebraically the squared distance between centers equals the sum of squared radii. Orthogonal circles are self-inverse, so inversion in one fixes the other as a set.

label: Inversive Distance
notes: For two non-intersecting circles the inversive distance is an invariant of the inversive group, computable from the centers and radii. Because it survives every inversion, it certifies when two coaxal configurations are genuinely equivalent and supplies a metric on the space of disjoint circles.

label: The Circle of Apollonius
notes: Fixing two points and a ratio of distances traces the Apollonius locus. When the ratio equals one the locus is the perpendicular bisector; for every other positive ratio it is a circle whose center and radius follow directly from the two points and the ratio.

label: Spheres and Stereographic Projection
notes: The same product rule defines inversion in a sphere. Stereographic projection is inversion of a tangent plane from the north pole onto the sphere: it is conformal, sends circles and lines to circles, and explains geometrically why the inverse plane needs one added point at infinity.

label: The Elliptic Plane
notes: Identifying antipodal points on a sphere yields the elliptic plane, whose lines are great circles. Gnomonic projection straightens those great circles into lines. Girard's formula gives the area of a spherical triangle as its angle excess, the area identity that survives antipodal identification.

label: Recap
notes: Power, radical axis, and coaxal pencils organize circles; inversion unifies lines and circles as one conformal family; inversive distance measures disjoint pairs; Apollonius turns a metric ratio into a circle; spheres extend everything to stereographic projection and the elliptic plane.
